title: Tile Side
statement: A carpenter wants to cut every plank in planks into equal pieces of one shared whole-number length, with no leftover wood on any plank. Return the longest piece length that works for every plank.

examples.explanation: Pieces of length 6 divide all three planks, and nothing longer does.

hints.content: The piece length must divide every plank length exactly.
No piece can be longer than the shortest plank, so you could try lengths from there downward.
The largest number dividing two numbers is their greatest common divisor, and gcd(a, b, c) = gcd(gcd(a, b), c).
Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), and gcd(a, 0) = a.
Fold the array with gcd, starting from the first plank.

testCases.explanation: Pieces of length 6 divide all three planks, and nothing longer does.
A single plank can stay whole.
A plank of length 1 forces length 1.
A large prime length still works when every plank is identical.

solutions.title: Try lengths from the shortest plank downward
solutions.intuition: The first length that divides every plank, counting down from the shortest plank, is the longest one.
solutions.approach: Let low be the shortest plank. For side from low down to 1, return side if every plank is divisible by it.
solutions.pseudocode: for side from min(planks) down to 1: if all p % side == 0: return side
commonMistakes: Starting from the longest plank, which wastes work and can return a length that does not divide the shortest plank.
Spreading a very large array into Math.min, which can exceed the call-argument limit in some engines.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Counting down from the shortest plank finds the answer, but it can test up to a million candidates against every plank.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For [12, 18, 30], start at 12: 18 % 12 is not 0. Try 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7, which all fail.

solutions.title: Fold with Euclid's algorithm
solutions.intuition: The answer is the greatest common divisor of all lengths, and gcd can be combined one plank at a time.
solutions.approach: Define gcd(a, b) by repeatedly replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b). Reduce the planks with it.
solutions.pseudocode: g = planks[0]; for p in planks[1:]: g = gcd(g, p); return g
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log M) for maximum length M
commonMistakes: Starting the fold at 0 without understanding why gcd(0, x) = x; starting from planks[0] is clearer.
Using subtraction-based gcd, which is far slower for unequal values.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A piece length must divide every plank, so the longest one is the gcd of the whole array. gcd is associative, so I fold it across the planks with Euclid's algorithm, which takes logarithmic steps per pair. That's O(n log M) time and constant space. I could also stop early once the running gcd hits 1.
